Ranking the survivors on growth and size then adjusts for growth expectations and the size-related risk premium, and the median keeps the estimate robust.
proposals.prediction: Exploration median error below 0.603 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2, band ebitda_margin±0.05 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 0.5 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> [band ebitda_margin±0.05]

proposals.name: L3 growth-risk-quality EBITDA peers, median
proposals.mechanism: In a DCF, EV/EBITDA rises with growth and with the quality of cash conversion (EBITDA margin) and falls with financial risk (net debt to EBITDA). Ranking 3-digit industry peers on these three drivers with a fairly large k, and taking the median, keeps the fundamental adjustment while staying close to the robust industry median.
proposals.prediction: Exploration median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, ebitda_margin 0.5, net_debt_to_ebitda 0.5 | k=20, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_growth_roic
proposals.mechanism: In a DCF framework the EV/EBITDA multiple is driven mainly by expected growth and by the return on capital that growth earns. Within a 3-digit industry, peers matched on recent sales growth and ROIC should share the same value-creation profile and therefore similar multiples.
proposals.prediction: Median absolute log error below the L3 industry-median baseline (0.333) in at least 3 of 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, roic 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_size
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA ignores reinvestment, so firms that spend heavily on capex turn less EBITDA into free cash flow and should trade at lower EV/EBITDA. Matching on capex intensity and size within the industry pairs firms with similar cash conversion and similar risk and liquidity.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gains in capital-intensive 2-digit sectors.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank capex_intensity 1, log_sales 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L2_margin_leverage
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA margin captures competitive position and how durable operating profit is, while net debt to EBITDA captures financial risk and distress costs, both of which affect the discount rate applied to EBITDA. A broader 2-digit pool gives enough candidates for these risk-and-quality neighbours to be close.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.340 overall, and lower than the Bhojraj-Lee warranted-multiple peers baseline (0.380) in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, net_debt_to_ebitda 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L3_margin_growth
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so peers with similar profitability per dollar of sales and similar growth should have similar sales multiples. Within a 3-digit industry this matching removes most of the margin spread that makes plain industry EV/Sales medians noisy.
proposals.prediction: Median error below the L3 industry-median baseline (0.603) in all 4 exploration years, by at least 0.05 on average.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L2_gross_ebitda_margin
proposals.mechanism: Gross margin reflects pricing power and the business model (for example software against distribution), and EBITDA margin reflects realised operating profitability. Together they place a firm on the value-per-sales-dollar curve, even across 3-digit industry lines inside a 2-digit sector.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, and beats the Bhojraj-Lee regression (0.674) in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank gross_margin 1, ebitda_margin 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L3_ebit_margin_turnover
proposals.mechanism: By the DuPont identity, sales multiples reflect return on capital, which is EBIT margin times asset turnover: high-turnover, low-margin firms trade at low EV/Sales. Matching on both pins down capital efficiency and profitability within the industry.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.580 overall and below the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebit_margin 1, asset_turnover 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: L2 growth-risk peers, median
proposals.mechanism: Within a broad industry, EV/EBITDA is driven mainly by expected growth and risk; matching on sales growth, return on capital and leverage selects peers with similar growth-adjusted cost of capital. Using a large k with the median instead of a harmonic mean of 10 removes the downward bias and noise from small, outlier-prone peer sets.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.name: L2 margin-matched sales peers
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so a firm's sales multiple scales almost one-for-one with its profitability. Picking same-sector peers nearest in EBITDA and gross margin captures this, and the median keeps a few high-multiple firms from dominating as they do under a mean.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.603 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 0.7, gross_margin 0.3 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Finest-industry median with cascade
proposals.mechanism: Firms in the same 4-digit SIC share products, customers and cost structure, so their EBITDA multiples cluster most tightly; the cascade to 3- and 2-digit groups only kicks in when the narrow group is too thin. Dropping the narrow growth band and the mean avoids throwing away good peers and being pulled by outliers.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l4 | k=all, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l3] -> [same industry_l2]

proposals.name: Industry plus margin band, median
proposals.mechanism: Because EV/Sales is roughly EV/EBITDA times margin, industry peers with nearly the same EBITDA margin should have nearly the same sales multiple. A hard margin band inside the industry, widening to the sector and then to all firms, keeps the margin match while ensuring enough peers.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.580 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.name: Cross-industry fundamentals twins
proposals.mechanism: Sales multiples depend on profitability, growth and gross-margin structure more than on SIC labels, so the nearest firms in margin and growth space, from any industry, should share the target's EV/Sales. Ranking the whole cross-section with a moderate k and median avoids the thin, noisy 4-digit groups of the earlier version.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.603 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.name: L3 size-growth peers, median
proposals.mechanism: Within a 3-digit industry, larger firms trade at lower risk premia and faster-growing firms at higher EBITDA multiples; matching on size and growth isolates peers with the same growth and discount-rate profile. A k of 20 with the median keeps the peer set close to the robust industry median while tilting it toward the most comparable firms.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 0.5 | k=20, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_growth_reinvestment_harmonic
proposals.mechanism: My strongest vote: EV/EBITDA is essentially a capitalization rate on cash flow, so within an industry the multiple should be set by growth (sales_growth_1y) and by how much of EBITDA must be reinvested (capex_intensity), with ROIC telling us whether that growth creates value. Industry membership controls for risk and accounting conventions, and ranking on these drivers inside it should beat the plain industry median. I use the harmonic mean because it averages the earnings yields rather than the multiples, which removes the upward bias of averaging ratios and is robust to a few very high multiples.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.320 overall and beats the L3/L2 industry median (0.333) in at least 3 of 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, capex_intensity 1, roic 0.5, log_sales 0.5 | k=8, harmonic_mean, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L2_growth_size_median
proposals.mechanism: A more conservative variant of the first idea: 2-digit SIC gives a larger pool, so the nearest-neighbour step has more real choice, and I rank only on the two drivers I trust most, growth and size (larger firms are less risky and command higher multiples). Using only well-covered features keeps peers from being dropped for missing data, and the median keeps it robust. If this does about as well as the richer recipe, the team should prefer it for the hold-out test.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| at or below 0.330 and beats the Bhojraj-Lee warranted-multiple peers (0.380) in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 1, ebitda_margin 0.5 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L4_leverage_cascade
proposals.mechanism: Firms in the same narrow 4-digit industry share business models most closely, but EV/EBITDA also moves with financial risk: highly levered firms tend to trade at lower enterprise multiples because of distress risk. This recipe starts as narrow as possible, widens step by step only when it has to, and ranks on net debt to EBITDA and growth. I expect it to help most in capital-heavy industries where leverage differs a lot between firms.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3/L2 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years; improvement concentrated in firms with net_debt_to_ebitda above the cross-sectional median.

proposals.mechanism: This is where I think the biggest gain is. EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so the industry median fails mainly because firms in an industry have very different margins. Ranking peers mostly on ebitda_margin inside the 2-digit industry, with growth as the second driver, directly fixes the main source of EV/Sales error. I expect a large improvement over the 0.603 baseline.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.50 overall and beats the L3/L2 industry median (0.603) in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 2, sales_growth_1y 1, gross_margin 0.5 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Sales_L3_margin_band_cascade
proposals.mechanism: This is a stricter form of margin matching: a hard band of plus or minus 5 points of EBITDA margin within the 3-digit industry guarantees that peers have similar profitability, and the ranking then sorts by growth and size. If the industry is too thin, it keeps the margin band but relaxes the industry, because for EV/Sales I believe profitability matters more than industry code. This tests whether a hard margin screen beats a soft margin ranking.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3/L2 industry median in all 4 years, with median |ln error| within 0.03 of Sales_L2_margin_matched.

proposals.name: Sales_crossindustry_fundamentals
proposals.mechanism: This is a contrarian bet worth one slot: for EV/Sales, a firm's margin, growth and capital intensity may predict its multiple better than its SIC code, which is often stale for diversified or newer firms. With no industry filter and a larger k, we find fundamental twins across the whole market, and the harmonic mean keeps high-multiple outliers from dominating. If it is competitive with the industry-based recipes, that tells the team that fundamentals and not industry labels should drive the next round.

Within a narrow 3-digit industry, matching on capex intensity, ROIC and net leverage finds peers that turn EBITDA into free cash flow at a similar rate and carry similar risk. The harmonic mean reduces the pull of outlier high multiples.

proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.333 and below the Bhojraj-Lee warranted-multiple baseline of 0.357, with the biggest gain in capital-intensive 2-digit sectors.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank capex_intensity 1, roic 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L2_size_growth
proposals.mechanism: Larger firms carry lower risk and better access to capital, which lowers their discount rate, and faster-growing firms earn higher multiples. A wider 2-digit pool gives the size-and-growth ranking enough candidates to find close matches.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error at or below 0.34, and a mean error below the L3 baseline mean of 0.513.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank log_sales 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sales_L3_margin_growth
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is roughly EV/EBITDA multiplied by the EBITDA margin, so differences in profitability drive most of the spread in sales multiples. Peers in the same 3-digit industry with similar EBITDA margins and similar growth should have similar EV/Sales.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.50, which beats the L3 industry-median baseline of 0.603 in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sales_L3_gross_ebit_margin
proposals.mechanism: Gross margin reflects pricing power and the business model, while EBIT margin reflects operating profitability after overhead and depreciation. Matching both identifies peers that turn a dollar of sales into similar long-run cash flow.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.52 and better than the Bhojraj-Lee warranted multiple (0.674) in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank gross_margin 1, ebit_margin 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sales_L2_margin_size
proposals.mechanism: Profitability sets how much value each dollar of sales supports, and size proxies for risk and market position. Searching across the broader 2-digit industry for firms close on EBITDA margin and size finds better economic twins than a narrow SIC code with few members.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.55, which beats the L3 industry-median baseline of 0.603 in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, log_sales 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sales-multiple via margin-matched industry peers
proposals.mechanism: My view: EV/Sales is mostly a margin multiple. EV/Sales is roughly EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so a peer with a similar margin in the same broad industry should trade at a similar sales multiple. The industry median ignores this, and I think that is why its EV/Sales error is nearly twice its EV/EBITDA error. Ranking 2-digit peers mainly on EBITDA margin, with growth and gross margin as tie-breakers, should close much of that gap. This is where I would put the most effort.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.52 on FY2016-2019, beating the EV/Sales industry median (0.603) in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Cross-industry margin band for EV/Sales
proposals.mechanism: This tests whether industry labels add anything once profitability is matched. The idea is that firms with the same EBITDA margin and a similar gross-margin structure turn a dollar of sales into similar cash flow, whatever their SIC code. If this matches or beats recipe 1, then SIC codes are mostly standing in for margins in sales multiples, and we can stop working on industry definitions for EV/Sales.
proposals.prediction: Beats the EV/Sales industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with a pooled median error within 0.03 of the margin-matched industry recipe.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen band ebitda_margin±0.05 | rank gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 0.5 | k=15, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [band ebitda_margin±0.1] -> []

proposals.name: Narrow-industry EV/Sales with margin ranking
proposals.mechanism: This is the tighter version of recipe 1: 3-digit industry peers, again ranked mostly on EBITDA margin, with a harmonic mean. Firms in the same narrow industry share a cost structure and similar investor expectations. The harmonic mean averages the inverse multiple (yield), so a few very richly priced peers cannot pull the estimate up. Unprofitable high-flyers inflate EV/Sales averages, so the harmonic mean should help most here.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.55 and mean error below 0.85 on FY2016-2019, beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.name: Growth-and-ROIC matched EV/EBITDA within industry
proposals.mechanism: In a growing-perpetuity model, EV/EBITDA is driven by growth, by how efficiently growth is funded (ROIC), and by risk. Within a 3-digit industry, risk is already roughly matched, so ranking on sales growth and ROIC should capture most of the remaining spread in multiples, and size adds a little for liquidity and risk. I would expect a modest gain, because the industry median for EV/EBITDA is already a strong baseline.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.32 on FY2016-2019, beating the EV/EBITDA industry median (0.333) in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 2, roic 1.5, log_sales 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Reinvestment-adjusted EV/EBITDA peers
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA overstates free cash flow most for capital-heavy firms. Two firms with the same EBITDA but different capex needs should trade at different multiples, and the one with heavy capex should get a lower multiple. Leverage matters too, because high net debt to EBITDA signals distress risk. Ranking 2-digit peers on capex intensity, growth and net debt to EBITDA targets the cash-conversion gap that the industry median ignores. The harmonic mean keeps hot peers from inflating the estimate.
proposals.prediction: Beats the EV/EBITDA industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with a mean error below 0.49, which is better than the Bhojraj-Lee warranted multiple.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank capex_intensity 2, sales_growth_1y 1.5, net_debt_to_ebitda 1, ebitda_margin 0.5 | k=12, harmonic_mean, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Finest-industry EV/EBITDA with cascading fallback
proposals.mechanism: This is a simple control. A 4-digit SIC code groups firms with nearly the same products, customers and cycle, so their EBITDA multiples should match more closely than 3-digit groups do. Falling back to 3-digit and then 2-digit codes keeps coverage up. If this alone beats the L3 baseline, industry granularity is worth exploiting before any feature ranking. If it does not, the ranking recipes are where the value is.
proposals.prediction: Median error between 0.315 and 0.335 and beats the L3 industry median in at least 2 of 4 years; I expect a small gain, not a large one.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l4 | k=all, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l3] -> [same industry_l2]

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_value_drivers

Matching peers in the same 3-digit SIC on ROIC, sales growth, leverage and size picks out firms whose discounted cash flow per unit of EBITDA should be closest to the target's.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below the L3/L2 industry median (0.333) in at least 3 of the 4 exploration years, and below 0.33 pooled.

Peers in the same 2-digit sector with similar capex intensity, EBITDA margin and growth should convert EBITDA to cash at similar rates and so trade at similar multiples.

Ranking all firms on these fundamentals lets the engine find economic peers that SIC codes misclassify.

proposals.mechanism: My read is that Recipe 1 lost to the baseline because it widened the pool to 2-digit SIC and then used a harmonic mean, which pulls the estimate toward low multiples. Holding risk constant, EV/EBITDA depends mostly on growth and on how much of EBITDA has to go back into capex, so I'd keep the 3-digit industry pool and rank on sales growth and capex intensity, with a little weight on margin and size. A median handles the right skew in multiples and fits a log-error metric better than a harmonic mean does.

proposals.name: L3 margin-matched EV/Sales, median
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is just EV/EBITDA times the EBITDA margin, so within an industry the margin is the biggest single driver of the sales multiple, much more than size or ROIC (which Recipe 2 used). Recipe 2 also averaged with a mean, and that gets dragged up by the few firms with very high multiples. I think matching on EBITDA margin, plus some gross margin and growth, inside the 3-digit industry and taking the median is the most promising direction for EV/Sales.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.603 and beats the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years; I expect an improvement of at least 0.04 over the baseline.

proposals.mechanism: The ±10% growth band in Recipe 3 was too tight: it emptied the peer pool and pushed many firms into the fallback. That fallback had no ranking at all, and its mean got distorted by outliers. My suggestion is a wide size band inside 2-digit SIC (roughly within a factor of 4.5 in sales), because size proxies for risk and the discount rate, and then ranking on growth and ROIC so that peers share the same value-creation profile. If too few peers survive, the recipe drops the size band but keeps the ranking.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.335, i.e. at least matching the industry median, and beats it in at least 2 of 4 years; coverage above 99%.

What sets EV/Sales is how many cents of operating profit each dollar of sales produces, and how fast sales are growing. I'd use the 2-digit pool so there are enough firms with close margins, and rank mostly on EBITDA margin and gross margin. A larger, margin-matched pool should beat a small 3-digit pool that isn't matched on margin.

proposals.mechanism: This tests whether a hard EBITDA-margin screen beats soft ranking. I keep only same-industry peers whose margin is within 5 points of the target's, since firms with similar margins should trade at similar sales multiples once the industry fixes the risk. Inside that band I rank on growth and margin. Recipe 5 failed because the 4-digit pool was thin, it ignored margin as a screen, and it used a mean.

proposals.mechanism: This is the simplest version and serves as a control. Firms in the same 4-digit SIC code share products, customers and cost structure more closely than 3-digit peers, so their EV/EBITDA should be closer. When fewer than 5 such firms exist, the recipe steps back to 3-digit and then 2-digit SIC. Matching on capex intensity and EBITDA margin within a 3-digit industry pairs firms with similar cash conversion and operating economics.

Operating margin reflects how much of that gross profit reaches investors. Firms that match on both have a similar cost structure and long-run profitability, which are the main drivers of value per dollar of sales, so a 2-digit pool gives enough candidates to find close matches.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.52 and below the industry-median baseline in at least 3 of the 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank gross_margin 1, ebit_margin 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sales: margin and capital intensity within 2-digit industry
proposals.mechanism: Value per dollar of sales depends on how much cash each dollar of sales throws off after reinvestment. That is roughly EBITDA margin minus capex intensity. Matching on both within the 2-digit industry gives peers with similar free-cash-flow margins and so similar EV/Sales multiples.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.53 and below the 0.674 warranted-multiple regression baseline in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, capex_intensity 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Industry growth-and-reinvestment neighbors (median)
proposals.mechanism: Within an industry, EV/EBITDA mostly reflects expected growth and how much of EBITDA must be reinvested (capex) instead of being paid out as free cash flow. Taking a 3-digit industry and then the firms closest on 1-year growth and capex intensity matches those two drivers. A median over a fairly large k keeps the estimate from being pulled around by a few extreme multiples, which is what hurt the harmonic-mean version.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.330 on the exploration years, beating the L3/L2 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with coverage of at least 99%.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, capex_intensity 0.5 | k=15, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Industry margin-matched EV/Sales
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so within an industry, firms with similar operating and gross margins should earn similar revenue multiples. Ranking 3-digit industry peers on EBITDA and gross margin targets the main reason EV/Sales differs across firms. A median, instead of the mean, guards against loss-making firms with very large multiples.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.580, beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 0.6, gross_margin 0.4 | k=12, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Industry value-driver neighbors: ROIC and growth
proposals.mechanism: In valuation theory, a firm's EV/EBITDA rises with growth, but only when the firm earns returns on invested capital above its cost of capital, so peers should match on ROIC and growth together. Ranking 3-digit industry peers on both, rather than screening on a narrow growth band, matches the value drivers without cutting the peer set down to noise. A wide k with a median aggregate keeps the estimate stable.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.335 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years; if it does not, ROIC adds nothing beyond the industry.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank roic 0.5, sales_growth_1y 0.5 | k=20, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Sector peers inside an EBITDA-margin band
proposals.mechanism: Leverage (debt to assets) does not explain EV/Sales; the margin earned on each dollar of revenue does. Taking 2-digit sector peers whose EBITDA margin is within 7 points of the target's, then ranking them on margin and growth, gives peers that turn a dollar of sales into similar cash flow. The broader sector filter keeps enough peers once the margin band is applied.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.590, beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2, band ebitda_margin±0.07 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 0.5 | k=10, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> [band ebitda_margin±0.05]

proposals.name: Industry margin and capital-intensity EV/Sales
proposals.mechanism: Firms that need many assets per dollar of revenue (low asset turnover) carry more enterprise value per dollar of sales, and gross and EBITDA margins set how much of each sale becomes cash flow. Matching 3-digit industry peers on margins and asset turnover covers both sides of the revenue multiple. The previous 4-digit filter left too few peers for this kind of matching, so the industry level is coarser here.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.590, beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank gross_margin 0.5, ebitda_margin 0.3, asset_turnover 0.2 | k=10, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Finest-industry median with cascading fallback
proposals.mechanism: Firms in the same 4-digit SIC code share products, customers, technology and regulation, so their EV/EBITDA multiples are pushed by the same growth and risk factors more than size or capex alone can capture. The rule uses the narrowest industry that has at least 5 peers and steps out to 3 and then 2 digits only when needed. This tests whether finer industry definition, rather than ranking on accounting features, is what beats the baseline.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.330, beating the L3/L2 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l4 | k=all, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l3] -> [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: L3 growth-capex neighbors, median
proposals.mechanism: Within a 3-digit industry, EV/EBITDA differs mostly because of expected growth and because EBITDA turns into free cash flow at different rates (capex intensity). Picking the industry peers closest on these two drivers, and taking a median so outliers have little effect, should keep the industry anchor while removing the growth and reinvestment differences that a plain industry median ignores.
proposals.prediction: Exploration median error below 0.333 (the industry median baseline), beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, capex_intensity 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

Ranking broad-industry peers on growth, ROIC and size, with a median, targets these fundamentals directly and avoids the noisy growth band and mean used before.

proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, roic 0.5, log_sales 0.5 | k=15, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

A tight EBITDA-margin band, then ranking on gross margin and growth with a median, captures the profitability and growth drivers of the multiple.
proposals.prediction: Exploration median error below 0.603, beating the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen band ebitda_margin±0.03 | rank gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 0.5 | k=15, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [band ebitda_margin±0.08] -> []

proposals.mechanism: Within a 3-digit industry, firms share technology and cost structure, and the EBITDA margin that remains is what maps their sales into enterprise value. Picking the few industry peers closest in EBITDA margin and taking a median should remove most of the margin spread in the industry median without the outlier sensitivity of the earlier mean.

Using the full 4-digit median when at least five peers exist, and stepping back to 3-digit and then 2-digit industries otherwise, adds precision only where enough peers support it.

Choosing L3 peers that are close on these drivers, and taking the median instead of the harmonic mean, holds on to the industry signal while removing the downward bias and outlier sensitivity that hurt Recipe 1.

proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so within an industry the sales multiple is driven mostly by profitability. Ranking L3 peers on EBITDA margin first and gross margin second (the pricing power behind future margins) matches the main source of variation in EV/Sales. proposals.mechanism: A hard growth band of +/-10% throws away too many real peers and adds noise. Ranking on growth inside L3 with a wide k keeps the robustness of an industry median and tilts the peer set toward firms with similar expected growth and operating scale economics (EBITDA margin), the two main drivers of EV/EBITDA in a constant-growth model.

proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, ebitda_margin 0.5 | k=20, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: Leverage does not set an enterprise-value multiple, but profitability does: two firms in the same industry with similar EBITDA margins should trade at similar EV/Sales. A margin band of +/-5 points inside L3, ranked on margin and growth, isolates those firms. The fallbacks widen first to L2 and then to the whole market, still margin-banded, so margin comparability is never dropped.

proposals.mechanism: 4-digit groups are often too thin, and the mean is pulled up by extreme sales multiples. A broader L2 pool gives enough candidates to match closely on EBITDA margin (the main EV/Sales driver), growth (capitalized future sales), and size (risk and maturity). A median over 12 peers is a stable central estimate.

With no feature ranking, all peers are used and the median is taken, which avoids the noise of size/capex matching. The search widens to L3 and then L2 only when the group has too few firms.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.330 and beats the L3/L2 industry median in at least 2 of 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l4 | k=all, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l3] -> [same industry_l2]

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_growth_capex_leverage
proposals.mechanism: My view is that the EV/EBITDA payoff comes from keeping the industry anchor and then matching on the three things the multiple capitalizes: growth, the capex drag that separates EBITDA from free cash flow, and leverage risk. Inside an industry these vary a lot, and a growth-plus-reinvestment match should take out the mismatches that a plain industry median leaves in. I'd focus effort here first because it builds on the strongest baseline, not against it.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.333 (industry median L3/L2) in at least 3 of 4 exploration years, with a pooled median of 0.32 or lower.

proposals.name: EBITDA_L2_profitability_harmonic
proposals.mechanism: Firms that earn similar returns on capital and are a similar size should trade at similar multiples of EBITDA, because ROIC governs how much value each unit of growth creates and size proxies for risk and liquidity. The broader 2-digit pool gives enough candidates for nearest-neighbour matching to work, and the harmonic mean is the right average for price ratios: it damps the high-multiple outliers that inflate arithmetic means.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.333 and pooled mean error below 0.50, beating the industry median on the mean in all 4 years.

proposals.name: EBITDA_fundamentals_no_industry
proposals.mechanism: This is the contrarian bet, and a test of whether SIC codes are needed at all: if the multiple really comes from growth, margin, reinvestment and risk, then cross-industry fundamental twins should do as well as industry peers. I expect it to come close to the industry baseline but not beat it clearly. That outcome would still be useful, because it tells us how much of the industry signal is fundamentals and how much is sector sentiment.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error between 0.32 and 0.37, i.e. within 0.04 of the industry median, and beats the Bhojraj-Lee peers (0.380) in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.name: Sales_L2_margin_matched
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is EV/EBITDA times the EBITDA margin, so most of the spread in sales multiples within an industry is margin, and matching on margin is the single biggest lever. This is where I think the largest gains are available to the team: the industry median ignores margin entirely, which is why its EV/Sales error is nearly twice its EV/EBITDA error. Gross margin and growth then sort out the remaining pricing-power and growth premium.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.52, beating the industry median (0.603) by at least 0.08 and in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Sales_margin_band_then_growth
proposals.mechanism: This is a stricter version of the margin idea: a hard ±5-point EBITDA-margin band keeps only peers with the same economics, and growth and size choose among them. When the industry pool is too thin, I would rather drop the industry than drop the margin match, because for a sales multiple margin carries more information than the SIC code. Harmonic averaging guards against a few richly valued peers.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.55 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years; the fallback cases (no industry) should have error no worse than 0.65.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2, band ebitda_margin±0.05 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 0.5, ebitda_margin 1 | k=8, harmonic_mean, min_peers=4 | fallback [band ebitda_margin±0.05] -> [same industry_l2]

proposals.name: Sales_cross_industry_economics
proposals.mechanism: Across industries, the sales multiple should mainly reflect profitability, how capital-light the business is, and growth. A capital-light, high-margin, fast-growing firm deserves a high EV/Sales whatever its SIC code, so twins on margin, asset turnover and growth should be good peers. I'd treat this as the EV/Sales counterpart of the no-industry test; my guess is it beats the industry median because margin dispersion dominates industry effects for this multiple.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.58, beating the industry median (0.603) in at least 3 of 4 years and the Bhojraj-Lee regression (0.674) in all 4.

Within a 2-digit SIC sector, which shares risk and accounting conventions, the nearest neighbors on growth, ROIC and margin should share the target's fundamental multiple more closely than a raw industry median does. Size is added at low weight as a proxy for risk and liquidity.

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_leverage_harmonic
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA leaves out capital spending, so firms that need heavy maintenance capex convert less EBITDA into free cash flow and trade at lower EV/EBITDA. Leverage is a proxy for risk and life-cycle stage. Matching narrow-industry peers on capex intensity, net debt/EBITDA and growth should capture this, and the harmonic mean limits the upward pull of a few peers with very high multiples (Baker-Ruback).
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median on median error in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gains in capital-intensive 2-digit sectors (e.g. utilities, energy, transport).

proposals.name: EBITDA_crossindustry_fundamentals_k20
proposals.mechanism: Valuation theory says the multiple depends on growth, profitability, reinvestment needs and risk, not on SIC codes, and SIC codes misclassify many firms. Ranking the whole cross-section on those drivers with a larger k gives a lower-variance warranted-multiple peer set. It also helps firms in thin or mixed industries, where industry medians rest on very few peers.

proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times the EBITDA margin, so the main cause of cross-firm differences in EV/Sales is profitability. Industry-median EV/Sales ignores this, which explains its much larger errors. Within a sector, peers matched mainly on EBITDA margin, and then on gross margin and growth, should remove most of that error.

proposals.mechanism: A hard band on EBITDA margin makes every peer's EV/Sales come from the same level of profitability, so the multiple differences that remain mostly reflect growth and capital intensity. Ranking inside the band on growth, asset turnover and capex should then pick out firms with similar cash-conversion economics, even across industries.

proposals.mechanism: EBITDA ignores the capital spending needed to sustain it, so firms with heavy capex convert less EBITDA to free cash flow and deserve a lower multiple. Matching industry peers on capex intensity and growth aligns both the cash conversion of EBITDA and its expected growth.

This is the cleanest theory-backed recipe in the set, so I expect it to hold up out of sample.

proposals.mechanism: Within an industry, EV/EBITDA is mainly driven by expected growth and by how durable the cash-flow margin is. Peers that match the target on both current EBITDA margin and 1-year sales growth should have similar discount rates and growth expectations, so their median multiple should be closer to the target's than the plain industry median.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln(V_est/V)| below the 0.333 L3 industry-median baseline in at least 3 of the 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_roic_growth
proposals.mechanism: Value-driver theory says the multiple of operating earnings rises with growth only when return on invested capital is above the cost of capital. Matching peers on ROIC and sales growth together captures that interaction, so peers with similar value created per dollar of growth should trade at similar EV/EBITDA.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.333 and below the Bhojraj-Lee warranted-multiple baseline (0.357) over FY2016-2019.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank roic 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_growth
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA leaves out the capital spending needed to keep operations running, so firms that spend heavily on capex turn less of their EBITDA into free cash flow and deserve lower EV/EBITDA. Matching on capex intensity adjusts for that reinvestment drag, and matching on growth separates capex that maintains the business from capex that expands it.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median's median error in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gain in capital-intensive 2-digit SIC groups.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank capex_intensity 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L3_margin_growth
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is roughly the EBITDA margin times EV/EBITDA, so it varies across firms mostly because margins differ, and then because growth differs. Picking same-industry peers with similar EBITDA margin and sales growth removes the biggest source of spread in revenue multiples.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln(V_est/V)| below 0.50, beating the 0.603 L3 industry-median baseline in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L3_gross_ebitda_margin
proposals.mechanism: Gross margin reflects pricing power and the long-run economics of the business model, and EBITDA margin reflects current operating efficiency. Peers that match on both have similar earnings per dollar of revenue now and similar room for margin gains later, so they should share an EV/Sales multiple.
proposals.prediction: Beats the 0.603 L3 industry-median baseline in at least 3 of 4 years and beats the Bhojraj-Lee warranted multiple (0.674) on the pooled median.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank gross_margin 1, ebitda_margin 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: A dollar of sales is worth more when it produces more operating profit and when the business earns high returns on the capital behind it. Using the broader 2-digit SIC group gives a larger candidate pool, so peers can be matched closely on EBIT margin and ROIC across related sub-industries with similar economics.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.603 and lower than the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebit_margin 1, roic 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

Peers from the same 3-digit industry that are closest on recent growth and ROIC should share the target's fundamental value drivers and so its multiple.

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_growth
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA overstates free cash flow by the amount of required capital spending, so firms with heavy capex should trade at lower EV/EBITDA than asset-light firms with the same EBITDA. Matching on capex intensity and growth within the industry pairs firms with similar cash conversion and similar growth prospects.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.333 and better than the Bhojraj-Lee warranted multiple (0.357) in at least 3 of 4 years.

proposals.mechanism: Size and financial leverage stand in for risk and cost of capital: larger, less levered firms have lower discount rates and more stable cash flows, so they earn higher EV/EBITDA. Peers close on log assets and net debt/EBITDA within the industry should have a similar discount rate.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gains among the smallest and most levered firms.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank log_assets 1, net_debt_to_ebitda 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: Firms in the same 3-digit industry share technology and demand cycles, and within that group similar size and EBITDA margin indicate a similar competitive position and similar risk. The harmonic mean is the right average for price multiples because it equally weights value per dollar of EBITDA, so it dampens peers with very high multiples.

Peers in the same broad industry with close EBITDA and gross margins and similar growth should have similar value per dollar of sales, which fixes the main weakness of an industry-median EV/Sales.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.50, clearly beating the 0.603 of the L3 industry median, in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Cross-industry profitability-and-growth twins (EV/Sales)
proposals.mechanism: If EV/Sales is driven mostly by margin, growth and the R&D intangibles that accounting expenses, then firms matched closely on those features should be valued alike even across SIC codes. Dropping the industry filter lets every firm in the year compete as a peer, which helps targets in thin or poorly coded industries.
proposals.prediction: Median error within 0.03 of the margin-matched L2 recipe and below the 0.603 industry-median baseline. If it does worse than the L2 version, industry membership carries information beyond these accounting features.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, rnd_intensity 1, sales_growth_1y 1, log_sales 0.5 | k=15, median, min_peers=3

proposals.name: L3 industry within a margin band (EV/Sales)
proposals.mechanism: A margin-conditioned industry median: within an industry, firms whose EBITDA margins are within 5 points of each other have about the same EBITDA per dollar of sales, so they should share the EV/Sales multiple. If the industry cell is too thin, the band is kept and the industry is widened step by step, so margin stays the main criterion.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median for EV/Sales in all 4 years by at least 0.05 in median error, with most of the gain for firms whose margins are far from their industry average.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3, band ebitda_margin±0.05 | k=all, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2, band ebitda_margin±0.05] -> [band ebitda_margin±0.03]

proposals.name: L2 growth-profitability neighbors, median
proposals.mechanism: Under a DCF, EV/EBITDA rises with expected growth and with return on capital (more value per unit of reinvestment). Peers in the same 2-digit sector with similar growth, ROIC and size should share discount rates and value-creation profiles. Using the median instead of the harmonic mean removes the downward bias that likely hurt the original recipe.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, roic 0.6, log_sales 0.4 | k=15, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: L2 margin-matched EV/Sales, median
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales equals EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so the margin drives most of the cross-sectional variation in sales multiples. Matching on EBITDA and gross margin within a broad sector picks peers that turn a dollar of sales into similar cash flow, and the median keeps high-multiple outliers from dominating.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.603 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, gross_margin 0.5, sales_growth_1y 0.3 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: L3 growth and leverage-risk peers, median
proposals.mechanism: Within a 3-digit industry, EV/EBITDA differences come mainly from growth expectations and risk; leverage relative to EBITDA is an accounting proxy for financial risk and maturity. Ranking on these without a hard growth band keeps peer sets large and stable, and the median is robust to transitory EBITDA dips.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 0.6, net_debt_to_ebitda 0.4 | k=20, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: L3 margin-and-size EV/Sales, median
proposals.mechanism: Inside a 3-digit industry, firms with similar EBITDA margins earn similar cash flow per dollar of sales, and similar size proxies for similar risk and market position. Replacing debt-to-assets with margin targets the main driver of the sales multiple, and the median handles skewed multiples.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.595 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 0.7, log_sales 0.3 | k=10, median, min_peers=4 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: Cross-industry fundamental EV/Sales twins
proposals.mechanism: A sales multiple is set by profitability, growth and capital needs rather than by the SIC label itself, so firms from any industry with matching EBITDA margin, gross margin, growth and capex intensity should have similar EV/Sales. Dropping the industry screen widens the pool so that close fundamental matches can be found, and a large k with the median keeps the estimate stable.
proposals.prediction: Median error below 0.603 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | rank ebitda_margin 1, gross_margin 0.5, sales_growth_1y 0.3, capex_intensity 0.2 | k=25, median, min_peers=5

proposals.name: L3 size-growth-margin peers, trimmed mean
proposals.mechanism: Firms of similar size within a 3-digit industry share liquidity and risk, and similar growth and margins indicate similar expected cash-flow paths, so they should trade at similar EBITDA multiples. A trimmed mean over a moderately large set keeps the information in the center of the distribution and removes the downward bias of the harmonic mean.
proposals.prediction: Median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank log_sales 0.5, sales_growth_1y 0.5, ebitda_margin 0.5 | k=15, trimmed_mean, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_growth_roic
proposals.mechanism: Under a steady-state DCF, EV/EBITDA rises with expected growth and with the return earned on reinvested capital, because high-ROIC firms need less reinvestment to fund the same growth. Matching on recent sales growth and ROIC inside the 3-digit industry pins down the two main fundamental drivers of the multiple, while the industry screen holds risk and accounting conventions roughly constant.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln(V_est/V)| below the L3/L2 industry-median baseline (0.333) in at least 3 of the 4 exploration years, and pooled below 0.325.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, roic 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_growth
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA leaves out capital spending, so two firms with the same EBITDA but different capex needs turn very different shares of EBITDA into free cash flow; capex-heavy firms should trade at lower EV/EBITDA. Matching on capex intensity corrects for that cash-conversion gap, and matching on sales growth captures the growth premium.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gains in capital-intensive 2-digit sectors (e.g., SIC 13, 28, 49).
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank capex_intensity 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_margin_size
proposals.mechanism: Larger firms with higher EBITDA margins tend to have more durable, lower-risk cash flows (scale advantages, market power, diversification), so they command a lower discount rate and a higher EV/EBITDA. Ranking on size and EBITDA margin within the 3-digit industry picks peers with similar risk and profitability positions.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error at or below 0.333 and beats the industry median in at least 2 of 4 years; mean error below 0.50.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, log_sales 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L3_margin_growth
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is roughly EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so margin is the main reason sales multiples differ across firms in the same industry; growth then sets the multiple applied to those margins. Matching on EBITDA margin and sales growth within the 3-digit industry captures both parts.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.50 (versus the 0.603 industry-median baseline), beating the baseline in all 4 exploration years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank ebitda_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: Gross margin reflects pricing power and the business model (e.g., software versus distribution), and EBIT margin reflects operating efficiency after overhead and depreciation; together they describe how much value each dollar of sales creates. Peers that match on both margins should have similar value per dollar of sales.

proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank gross_margin 1, ebit_margin 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: Within a broad 2-digit sector, a firm's EV/Sales is set mainly by its profitability per dollar of sales and by how efficiently it turns capital into profit, since ROIC decides how much value growth creates. Using the wider L2 pool lets the ranking find closer matches on margin and ROIC than a thin 3-digit industry could.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.53 and beats the industry median in at least 3 of 4 years; it does better than the L3 recipes in sparsely populated industries.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, roic 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_growth_roic

Within a 3-digit industry, peers that match the target on both recent sales growth and ROIC should share its value-creation profile and so its multiple.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln(V_est/V)| below the L3 industry-median baseline (0.333) in at least 3 of 4 exploration years, with the pooled median at or below 0.320.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, roic 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA_L3_capex_margin
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA ignores the capital spending needed to sustain it, so firms with high capex intensity turn less of each EBITDA dollar into free cash flow and should trade at lower EV/EBITDA. Matching peers on capex intensity and EBITDA margin within the industry lines up how much of EBITDA reaches investors as cash.

proposals.mechanism: Larger firms have lower risk (more diversified, cheaper capital, more liquid), which supports higher multiples. Margin level shows market position and how steady earnings are. Within an industry, peers that are close in size and EBITDA margin should face a similar discount rate and similar earnings durability.
proposals.prediction: Beats the L3 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years, with the pooled median between 0.31 and 0.33.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank log_sales 1, ebitda_margin 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales factors into EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so margin is the main driver of a sales multiple, and growth decides how much future sales are worth today. Within-industry peers matched on EBITDA margin and sales growth should share both parts of the multiple.

proposals.mechanism: Gross margin shows pricing power and how scalable the business model is (for example software versus distribution), and EBITDA margin shows current operating profitability. Peers that match on both have similar economics per sales dollar and should command a similar price per dollar of sales.

proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l3 | rank gross_margin 1, ebitda_margin 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: SALES_L2_margin_roic
proposals.mechanism: A sales multiple capitalizes margin times the value of reinvestment, and ROIC sets how much value each reinvested dollar creates. A broader 2-digit industry pool lets the nearest-neighbor step find peers that truly match on EBITDA margin and ROIC, rather than being stuck with a thin 3-digit group.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median error below 0.56, with the largest gains over the L3 industry median in industries where the L3 group has fewer than 10 firms.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 1, roic 1 | k=12, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA: industry peers matched on growth, reinvestment and return on capital
proposals.mechanism: My view is that EV/EBITDA is mostly a capitalized-cash-flow multiple, so within an industry it should vary with growth, how much of EBITDA must be reinvested (capex intensity), and how productively capital is used (ROIC). An L3 industry median ignores all three. Ranking same-industry firms on these value drivers and taking the median of the nearest 10 should keep the industry's shared risk and accounting norms while removing the largest within-industry differences in fundamentals. I think this is the most promising direction for EBITDA.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.320 pooled over FY2016-2019, and beats the L3/L2 industry median in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l3 | rank sales_growth_1y 1, capex_intensity 1, roic 1 | k=10, median, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l2] -> []

proposals.name: EBITDA: industry peers matched on size, leverage and margin
proposals.mechanism: Larger firms trade at higher EBITDA multiples because they are less risky and more liquid. Leverage changes how risky the equity is and how much of EV comes from debt, and a high margin signals pricing power that tends to last. Matching on these three within the 2-digit industry gives a peer set with similar risk, without making the industry definition so narrow that peer counts collapse. I expect a moderate gain, mainly from fixing small-firm and highly levered outliers.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.330 pooled, and mean |ln error| below the industry-median baseline mean of 0.513.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l2 | rank log_sales 1, net_debt_to_ebitda 1, ebitda_margin 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: EBITDA: narrow-industry harmonic mean cascade
proposals.mechanism: This is the simple control I would want on the table. Firms in the same 4-digit SIC share products, customers and cost structures most closely. The harmonic mean is the theoretically correct way to average price-scaled multiples, because it averages the yield (EBITDA/EV) and so is not pulled up by a few firms with very high multiples. Falling back to L3 and then L2 when the L4 group is thin keeps coverage. If this matches the fundamentals-ranked recipes, that tells us industry definition and aggregation matter more than peer ranking.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| at or below 0.330 pooled, and beats the L3 median baseline in at least 2 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/EBITDA | screen same industry_l4 | k=all, harmonic_mean, min_peers=5 | fallback [same industry_l3] -> [same industry_l2]

proposals.name: Sales: industry peers matched on profitability
proposals.mechanism: EV/Sales is roughly EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so the margin gap between firms is the main reason sales multiples differ inside an industry. An industry median that ignores margin will badly misvalue both low-margin and high-margin firms. Ranking L2 peers with a heavy weight on EBITDA margin, plus gross margin and growth, should remove most of that error. This is where I expect the largest improvement of all six recipes.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.500 pooled (versus 0.603 for the industry median), and beats the baseline in all 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | screen same industry_l2 | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1 | k=8, median, min_peers=5 | fallback []

proposals.name: Sales: cross-industry margin-and-growth twins
proposals.mechanism: I suspect that for sales multiples, economic similarity matters more than SIC code: a firm with a 30% EBITDA margin growing 15% a year should trade at a similar EV/Sales whatever its 2-digit code, and SIC codes are often stale. Dropping the industry screen and matching across the whole market on margins, growth and capex intensity tests whether value-driver similarity alone beats industry membership. A larger k of 20 offsets the noise from looser economic links.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.560 pooled, beating the industry median and the Bhojraj-Lee warranted multiple (0.674) in at least 3 of 4 years.
proposals.compact: EV/Sales | rank ebitda_margin 3, gross_margin 1, sales_growth_1y 1, capex_intensity 1 | k=20, median, min_peers=3

proposals.name: Sales: industry plus hard margin band
proposals.mechanism: This combines the two ideas above in a stricter form. It requires peers to share the industry and to have an EBITDA margin within 5 points of the target's, then picks among them by growth and size. A hard band guarantees that no peer has a very different margin, which a soft ranking cannot guarantee when the industry is thin. The fallbacks widen to L2 and then to a margin band only, so every firm still gets a margin-consistent peer set.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.520 pooled, and lower mean |ln error| than the industry-median baseline (0.945) in every year.

Peers close on both within a 3-digit industry should share the target's EV/Sales.

proposals.name: Sales_L2_margin_rnd
proposals.mechanism: R&D is expensed, so research-intensive firms report low current margins but are valued on future margins. Matching on EBITDA margin and R&D intensity within the broader 2-digit pool separates mature cash generators from investment-phase innovators that trade at high sales multiples despite thin current profits.
proposals.prediction: Pooled median |ln error| below the L3 industry median (0.603) in at least 3 of 4 years, with the largest gain among firms with R&D intensity above 5%.

Tightening the industry screen from L2 to L3 keeps peers with similar business risk, and the median avoids the downward pull the harmonic mean had in Recipe 1.

The median keeps the right-skewed sales multiples of loss-making or high-growth outliers from taking over the estimate.

Ranking on growth and ROIC rather than banding on growth avoids the thin, noisy peer sets that hurt Recipe 3, and the median resists outliers.

Matching on EBITDA margin, gross margin and R&D intensity inside L3 captures both current and latent profitability, and the harmonic mean reduces the upward bias of averaging ratios.

proposals.mechanism: My view is that industry membership already gets you most of the way on EV/EBITDA, and what's left over is mostly growth and how much of EBITDA actually becomes free cash flow. Within a 3-digit SIC group I'd rank on 1-year sales growth, capex intensity (EBITDA overstates cash for capital-heavy firms) and ROIC (value created per dollar reinvested), which are the drivers in a standard DCF-implied EBITDA multiple. I'd focus here first because it changes the industry median the least, so whatever it gains should be real and should hold up out of sample.

proposals.mechanism: SIC codes are crude, and I think a firm's EBITDA multiple depends on its economics more than on its label: growth, reinvestment needs, return on capital, R&D (expensed investment that holds down current EBITDA) and leverage risk. Dropping the industry screen and taking the 15 nearest firms on these features tests whether fundamentals can stand in for industry. I'd treat it as a real alternative bet, not a tweak. If it comes close to the industry recipes, that tells us the features carry most of the information.

Matching on size and growth inside L2 gives a larger, more stable peer pool than L3. The harmonic mean is the theoretically right way to average price multiples and limits the pull from a few extreme peers. I expect it to do slightly worse than the L3 recipe at the median but to be more robust in the tails.

Industry median EV/Sales fails mainly because it groups high-margin and low-margin firms together. Ranking L3 peers mainly on EBITDA margin, then gross margin (pricing power) and growth, should remove most of that dispersion. This is where I'd expect the biggest gain over a baseline across all six recipes, so it should get priority.

proposals.name: Sales multiple via margin-matched industry peers
proposals.mechanism: My strongest vote is here: EV/Sales is just EV/EBITDA times EBITDA margin, so the main reason the industry-median EV/Sales does so badly (0.603) is that it ignores how much of each sales dollar turns into cash flow. I think keeping the 2-digit industry screen to hold business model roughly fixed, then ranking mainly on EBITDA margin with gross margin and growth as secondary terms, should remove most of that error. I would put the team's EV/Sales effort into this direction first.

proposals.name: Sales multiple via cross-industry margin band
proposals.mechanism: I suspect for EV/Sales the margin profile matters more than the SIC code, because two firms with the same EBITDA margin and growth should get similar revenue multiples even in different industries. This recipe drops the industry screen, hard-bands on EBITDA margin, and ranks on gross margin, growth and asset turnover to capture business-model similarity. If it beats the industry-anchored version, that tells us SIC codes are a weak proxy for the drivers that matter.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.56 and beats the EV/Sales industry median in at least 3 of 4 years; it should do relatively better than the industry-anchored margin recipe for firms in sparse 3-digit industries.

proposals.name: Sales multiple, narrow industry plus margin, harmonic aggregation
proposals.mechanism: This tests the same margin idea inside the tighter 3-digit industry, with the harmonic mean, which works better for price-type ratios because it doesn't let a few very expensive peers pull the estimate up. I expect narrow industry plus margin matching to work well where the industry has enough members, and to fall back to 2-digit when it doesn't. It is a robustness check on proposal 1, not a separate bet.
proposals.prediction: Median |ln error| below 0.54 and within 0.03 of the L2 margin-matched recipe; beats the EV/Sales industry median in all 4 years.

proposals.name: EBITDA multiple via growth, reinvestment and return matching
proposals.mechanism: Because EBITDA already captures profitability, what is left in EV/EBITDA comes from growth, how much EBITDA goes back into capex, and the return earned on that reinvestment. That is the core of a DCF-based warranted multiple. My view is that ranking 2-digit industry peers on these three drivers, plus a little size for risk, is a better use of the industry baseline than the Bhojraj-Lee regression, which did worse than the plain industry median. I would make this the main EV/EBITDA direction.

proposals.name: EBITDA multiple via narrow industry, size and leverage
proposals.mechanism: Within a 3-digit industry, I think the main thing that sets multiples apart is risk: small firms and highly levered firms trade at lower EV/EBITDA because they are more likely to fail and have higher costs of capital. This recipe keeps the narrow industry screen behind the strongest baseline and ranks peers on size and net leverage. It is the conservative bet and is unlikely to do much worse than the baseline.

proposals.name: EBITDA multiple via quality-matched peers, trimmed aggregation
proposals.mechanism: EBITDA quality is different across firms: high gross margin, low capex firms turn more of their EBITDA into free cash flow and earn premium multiples, while asset-heavy firms don't. This ranks 2-digit industry peers on gross margin, capex intensity and asset turnover and uses a trimmed mean so it keeps more peer information than the median while dropping outliers. If it beats proposal 4, the team should focus on cash conversion rather than growth.
